#### Familiar Prompt If the prompt asks you to **\"Generate a Topic Map for [person name] with familiar prompt\"** or **\"Generate a Topic Map for / with familiar prompt\"** or **\"Generate a Topic Map with familiar prompt\"** you must: ## Act as a Topic Map Generator --- ### Purpose You are a **Topic Map Generator**, an AI system designed to analyze a user’s recent interactions with <entity referenceId=\"${smtp}\" id=\"${smtp}\">${name}</entity> and generate a structured, factual, and comprehensive summary in JSON format. The purpose of the Topic Map is to help the user quickly understand what’s been discussed, decided, or shared with that person, surfacing the **most current, relevant, and interconnected insights** across all communication channels. The Topic Map provides an instant, organized view of the relationship context — serving as a preparation and recall tool before meetings, follow-ups, or ad-hoc conversations. --- ### Role & Identity You have access to the user’s enterprise interactions — including chats, group chats, meetings, meeting notes, emails, and shared files. Your task is to identify, cluster, and summarize **key themes and takeaways** from these interactions. You must: - Focus on **topics** rather than specific files or events. - Merge signals from multiple channels when they refer to the same idea. - Reflect the **current state of collaboration** — what’s ongoing, recently updated, or important to remember. - Avoid speculation or inferred opinions. - Output one and only JSON object, and not include any text, commentary, or explanations outside of the JSON structure --- ### Core Objectives 1. **Summarize factual content only.** - Include only information explicitly present in recent data. - No opinions, emotions, or speculation. 2. **Prioritize active and recent topics.** - Emphasize what is still ongoing, unresolved, or evolving. - Deprioritize closed, completed, or finalized discussions. 3. **Synthesize across sources.** - Combine relevant information from multiple chats, meetings, or files when they relate to the same topic. - Present unified summaries rather than isolated fragments. 4. **Provide contextual follow-ups.** - Each bullet should include a `commandText` that invites the AI to explore or summarize *the latest and most relevant updates* about that topic. --- ### CommandText Design Principles Each `commandText` should be a **human-readable, topic-centered instruction** that guides the AI to synthesize insights about a theme across all relevant sources. It is not a query for a single file or meeting — it is a *semantic request for the system to gather the most recent and comprehensive view* of a topic. Each `commandText` must: - Reference **the target person** using the format `<entity type=\"People\" ReferenceId=\"personEmail\">Full Name<&#47;entity>`. - Clearly describe **the topic or subject** (e.g., roadmap planning, hiring strategy, onboarding experience). - Indicate **recency scope** (e.g., “recently,” “in the past month,” “this quarter”). - Start with a clear directive verb that defines the intent (e.g., “summarize,” “recap,” “highlight,” “explain,” “show what’s changed”). - End with the phrase “Begin with a TL;DR.” so responses always start with a short summary before elaborating on key points. --- ### Example CommandText - “Summarize the latest discussions with <entity type=\\\"People\\\" ReferenceId=\\\"anarodriguez@microsoft.com\\\">Anna Rodriguez<&#47;entity> about roadmap priorities and design trade-offs in the past month. Begin with a TL;DR.” - “Highlight recent updates and decisions discussed with <entity type=\\\"People\\\" ReferenceId=\\\"alex.kim@microsoft.com\\\">Alex Kim<&#47;entity> regarding budget alignment and vendor selection. Begin with a TL;DR.” - “Explain the current risks and dependencies identified in conversations with <entity type=\\\"People\\\" ReferenceId=\\\"priya.shah@microsoft.com\\\">Priya Shah<&#47;entity> about the AI onboarding experience. Begin with a TL;DR.” --- ### Output Format (Strictly Enforced) ```json { \"pillText\": \"[Person Name]\", \"commandText\": \"\", \"children\": [ { \"pillText\": \"[Theme or Topic]\", \"commandText\": \"\", \"children\": [ { \"pillText\": \"[Subtopic or Insight]\", \"children\": [ { \"pillText\": \"[Bullet-level insight]\", \"commandText\": \"[Full semantic follow-up query or instruction]\" } ] } ] } ] } ``` --- ### Example Output ```json { \"pillText\": \"Anna Rodriguez\", \"commandText\": \"\", \"children\": [ { \"pillText\": \"Product Strategy & Execution\", \"commandText\": \"\", \"children\": [ { \"pillText\": \"Q1 Priorities & Timeline\", \"children\": [ { \"pillText\": \"Agreed to prioritize retention and engagement metrics for Q1\", \"commandText\": \"Summarize the latest discussions with <entity type=\\\"People\\\" ReferenceId=\\\"anarodriguez@microsoft.com\\\">Anna Rodriguez<&#47;entity> about Q1 retention and engagement priorities, and highlight any recent changes in direction. Begin with a TL;DR.\" }, { \"pillText\": \"Delayed mobile redesign to Q2 to focus resources on core platform stability\", \"commandText\": \"Recap the most recent updates with <entity type=\\\"People\\\" ReferenceId=\\\"anarodriguez@microsoft.com\\\">Anna Rodriguez<&#47;entity> about the mobile redesign postponement and the current plan for Q2. Begin with a TL;DR.\" } ] }, { \"pillText\": \"User Research & Insights\", \"children\": [ { \"pillText\": \"Reported friction in enterprise onboarding process\", \"commandText\": \"Explain the latest insights and recommendations shared by <entity type=\\\"People\\\" ReferenceId=\\\"anarodriguez@microsoft.com\\\">Anna Rodriguez<&#47;entity> regarding onboarding friction for enterprise users in recent research or meetings. Begin with a TL;DR.\" } ] } ] } ] } ``` --- ### Recency & Relevance Heuristics - Prioritize **active, evolving discussions** over older, resolved ones. - Emphasize **what’s changed recently** — new updates, risks, or decisions. - Include **historical context** only when it clarifies the current state. - Recognize resolution cues like “approved,” “finalized,” or “completed” and deprioritize them. - Apply recency decay — favor insights from the last two weeks. --- ### Behavior & Output Rules - Do not infer or speculate — include only factual statements. - Merge signals across channels when they relate to the same theme. - Avoid redundancy and repetition. - Always maintain valid JSON structure. - Do not output anything outside the JSON object. --- ### Tone & Language - Factual, neutral, and professional. - No speculation, emotion, or interpretation. - Write concise, clear, and well-structured text. - Always in English. --- ### ✅ Quality Checklist A high-quality Topic Map output must: 1. Reflect **current, relevant, and factual** topics of collaboration. 2. Capture **cross-entity context** rather than isolated details. 3. Generate **topic-centric, context-rich commandText** instructions. 4. Be **readable, structured, and actionable** for the user. 5. I’ve read all three documents you uploaded. Here’s a quick summary of what each one covers:

2. Unleashing the Power of React

  • Course Overview: Focused on React fundamentals using React 18, assumes basic JavaScript knowledge.
  • Problems React Solves: Dynamic UI updates are hard with plain HTML/JS; React introduces structure and maintainability.
  • Structure with Components: React apps are built from reusable, hierarchical components.
  • Three Key Capabilities:
    1. Component-based structure.
    2. Declarative UI in JavaScript (via JSX).
    3. Efficient updates using reconciliation.

3. Application Anatomy

  • Components and JSX: Components are JS functions returning JSX, which Babel transforms into JS for React DOM.
  • Composition: Components can nest and form a hierarchy starting from a root component.
  • Tools: Next.js and Create React App provide preconfigured environments; JSX requires Babel.
  • Project Setup: Steps for creating a Next.js app, project structure, and running the dev server.
  • Modules: How ES modules work (export/import), default vs named exports.
  • Adding Components: Creating new components, importing them, and integrating into the app.
  • Debugging: Using ESLint, VS Code debugger, Chrome DevTools, and React Developer Tools.

4. Styling Components

  • Styling Options:
    • Global CSS (loaded via HTML or Next.js _document.js).
    • CSS classes applied via className.
    • CSS Modules for component-scoped styles.
    • Inline styles using the style attribute (discouraged for performance and maintainability).
  • Bootstrap Integration: Installing and using Bootstrap for layout.
  • CSS Modules: Scoped styles with unique class names via Webpack.
  • Best Practices: Prefer external CSS files over inline styles for performance and separation of concerns.

Awesome—here’s Hands‑On Lab Assignment #1 for your first doc, “Unleashing the Power of React.”
This lab is designed for candidates to implement missing pieces in a small React app that demonstrates component structure, JSX, declarative UI, and efficient updates. It includes stubs, TODOs, explanatory comments, and tests.

Note on tooling & style
• I’ve used CommonJS (require, module.exports) throughout to match your preference.
• Tests use Jest + React Testing Library (CJS-friendly). If you want a Vitest variant later, I can provide it in the next step.

Lab 1 — Build a Tiny Componentized UI (React Fundamentals)

🎯 Learning objectives

By the end of this lab, candidates will be able to:

  1. Explain the problems React solves for dynamic UIs and how components bring structure.
  2. Create simple function components that return JSX.
  3. Compose components to form a UI and handle parent/child communication via props.
  4. Manage local state in components.
  5. Observe and reason about efficient re-renders using a memoized child.

⏱️ Estimated time

60–90 minutes

<!-- README.md -->
# React Fundamentals Lab: Components, JSX & Efficient Updates

## Goals
Implement TODOs in components to pass all tests:
- Create and compose function components.
- Use JSX & props to build a UI.
- Manage local state.
- Prevent unnecessary re-renders with `React.memo`.

## Install & Run
```bash
npm i
npm test
# or
npm run test:watch

What you will build

A tiny UI that shows a header and either:

  • a HouseList (click a house to view details), or
  • HouseDetails for a selected house (with a local "Favorite" counter).

A memoized StaticBadge illustrates how React updates only what changed.


---

## Code Stubs with TODOs & Explanatory Comments

> Candidates: fill in **every `TODO`** and read comments carefully.

```js
// src/data/houses.js
// Basic seed data to keep the UI predictable for tests
module.exports = [
  { id: 1, address: '12 Ocean View', city: 'San Diego', price: 950000 },
  { id: 2, address: '44 Rosewood Lane', city: 'Austin',    price: 650000 },
  { id: 3, address: '7 Maple Street',  city: 'Boston',    price: 720000 }
];
JSX
// src/components/Header.jsx

// __tests__/app.spec.js
const React = require('react');
const { render, screen, fireEvent } = require('@testing-library/react');
const App = require('../src/App.jsx');

describe('React Fundamentals Lab', () => {
test('renders header with provided title', () => {
// We render App and then replace Header title by querying UI since App should pass a title
render(React.createElement(App));
const header = screen.getByTestId('app-header');
expect(header).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(header).toHaveTextContent(/globomantics/i); // loose match
});

test('shows list of houses and can navigate to details', () => {
render(React.createElement(App));

// Initially we should see 3 list items (house-1, house-2, house-3)
const first = () => screen.getByTestId('house-1');
const second = () => screen.getByTestId('house-2');
const third = () => screen.getByTestId('house-3');

expect(first()).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(second()).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(third()).toBeInTheDocument();

// Click the second house
fireEvent.click(second());

// Should now be in details view, showing address/city/price and a Back button
expect(screen.getByText(/house details/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(screen.getByText(/44 Rosewood Lane/)).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(screen.getByText(/Austin/)).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(screen.getByText(/\$?\s*650000/)).toBeInTheDocument();

// Favorite counter increments
const favCount = screen.getByTestId('fav-count');
expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent('0');
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/favorite/i));
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/favorite/i));
expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent('2');

// Back to list
fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/^back$/i));
expect(first()).toBeInTheDocument(); // list again
});

test('memoized StaticBadge does not re-render on unrelated parent state updates', () => {
render(React.createElement(App));

// Initial render count of badge should be "1"
const badgeCount = () => screen.getByTestId('badge-renders');
expect(badgeCount()).toHaveTextContent('1');

// Click parent "Tick" button a few times
const tickBtn = screen.getByTestId('tick');
fireEvent.click(tickBtn);
fireEvent.click(tickBtn);
fireEvent.click(tickBtn);

// Badge should still display render count "1" if memoized and props unchanged
expect(badgeCount()).toHaveTextContent('1');

// Parent ticks text should reflect increments
expect(screen.getByTestId('ticks').textContent).toBe('3');
});

test('handles empty houses gracefully (defensive check)', () => {
// Render HouseList in isolation by mocking App?
// Instead, verify the App-level flow: simulate an empty state by temporarily
// replacing the list would require dependency injection; so this test is
// about component-level guard. We’ll render HouseList directly.
const HouseList = require('../src/components/HouseList.jsx');
const { container } = render(React.createElement(HouseList, { houses: [], onSelect: () => {} }));
expect(screen.getByTestId('empty')).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(container).toMatchSnapshot();
});
});

1) Scaffold a fresh Next.js + TypeScript project

Shell
# Create the project (interactive; accept defaults or adjust as you like)
npx create-next-app@latest react-fundamentals-lab --typescript

# Move into the project
cd react-fundamentals-lab

# (optional) If you prefer Yarn or pnpm, initialize accordingly
# pnpm install
# or
# yarn install

The wizard will generate an App Router project using /app by default (Next.js 13+). That’s perfect for our labs.

2) Install testing stack (Jest + RTL) for Next.js (TS)

Next.js provides an official Jest preset via next/jest.

Shell
# Add test deps
npm i -D jest @types/jest ts-jest @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom @testing-library/user-event whatwg-url

Create jest.config.ts at the repo root:

TypeScript
// jest.config.ts
import nextJest from 'next/jest.js';

const createJestConfig = nextJest({
dir: './', // path to Next.js app
});

const customJestConfig = {
testEnvironment: 'jsdom',
setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
testMatch: ['**/__tests__/**/*.test.(ts|tsx)'],
// Allow absolute imports from src/ if you enable paths in tsconfig
moduleNameMapper: {
'^@/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/$1',
},
};

export default createJestConfig(customJestConfig);

Add jest.setup.ts:

TypeScript
// jest.setup.ts
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';

Update package.json scripts:

JSON with Comments
{
"scripts": {
"dev": "next dev",
"build": "next build",
"start": "next start",
"test": "jest --runInBand",
"test:watch": "jest --watch"
}
}

3) TypeScript config (paths optional)

The Next scaffold includes tsconfig.json. If you want a nice @/ alias, enable it:

JSON with Comments
// tsconfig.json (add these fields if missing)
{
"compilerOptions": {
"baseUrl": ".",
"paths": {
"@/*": ["*"]
}
}
}

Good catch—this failure is due to the test querying text /favorite/i, which matches both the button label “Favorite” and the paragraph label “Favorites: …”. Testing Library is telling us there are multiple matches.

There are two clean fixes. I recommend Fix A (test-only) because it mirrors how users interact (by role & accessible name) and avoids changing your UI copy.

✅ Fix A — Make the test target the button role (preferred)

Update the failing test lines in __tests__/app.test.tsx to query the button explicitly:

Diff
- fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/favorite/i));
- fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/favorite/i));
+ fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /favorite/i }));
+ fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /favorite/i }));

Why this works:

  • getByRole('button', { name: /favorite/i }) fetches the interactive control with accessible name “Favorite”, ignoring non-interactive text like “Favorites: …”.

Run tests again:

Shell
npm test

Option B — Add a test id to the button (UI change)

If you prefer not to touch the test, you can make the UI unambiguous by tagging the button and target that in the test:

In app/components/HouseDetails.tsx:

Diff
- <button onClick={() => setFavorites((f) => f + 1)}>Favorite</button>
+ <button data-testid="favorite-btn" onClick={() => setFavorites((f) => f + 1)}>
+ Favorite
+ </button>

In the test:

Diff
- fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/favorite/i));
- fireEvent.click(screen.getByText(/favorite/i));
+ fireEvent.click(screen.getByTestId('favorite-btn'));
+ fireEvent.click(screen.getByTestId('favorite-btn'));

Quick sanity rerun

After Fix A (or B):

Shell
npm test

You should see all tests pass:

  • ✅ renders header with provided title
  • ✅ shows list of houses and can navigate to details
  • ✅ memoized StaticBadge does not re-render on unrelated parent updates
  • ✅ HouseList handles empty array gracefully

Why Testing Library encourages role-based queries

  • Role queries (like getByRole('button', { name: /favorite/i })) follow accessible‑first testing and reduce ambiguity compared to getByText.
  • When multiple elements share similar text, role + name targets the interactive element users actually click.

You’re right—this failure is coming from the test logic, not the component.

In your failing test you’re asserting "2" after only one click. From your snippet:

TypeScript
expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent("0");
fireEvent.click(screen.getByTestId("favorite-btn"));
expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent("2"); // <-- expects 2 after 1 click
// then you click again (line duplicated) and assert 2 again

✅ Fix the test: click twice before asserting 2

Update the “navigate to details” test to perform two clicks on the Favorite button before expecting the count to be 2. Also, let’s keep the earlier improvement (target the button by test id or role).

Diff
- expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent("0");
- fireEvent.click(screen.getByTestId("favorite-btn"));
- expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent("2");
- fireEvent.click(screen.getByTestId("favorite-btn"));
- expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent("2");

+ // starts at 0
+ expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent("0");
+
+ // click twice -> expect 2
+ fireEvent.click(screen.getByTestId("favorite-btn"));
+ fireEvent.click(screen.getByTestId("favorite-btn"));
+ expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent("2");

If you switched to role-based querying earlier (also fine), use:

TypeScript
const favBtn = screen.getByRole('button', { name: /favorite/i });
fireEvent.click(favBtn);
fireEvent.click(favBtn);
expect(favCount).toHaveTextContent('2');

Why the failure occurred

  • The component increments the local favorites state by 1 per click:
    TypeScript
    <button onClick={() => setFavorites(f => f + 1)}>Favorite</button>
  • The test expected the count to jump to 2 after the first click, which is incorrect. Once you perform two clicks before the assertion, the test will pass.
